opus-5.5.text:
I think it can be a really good path, honestly. A lot of what makes someone effective on an alignment team isn't specific alignment knowledge. It's being a strong engineer in a modern ML stack. Can you work with large codebases? Can you debug a training run that's silently going wrong? Can you set up experiments cleanly, iterate quickly, and tell whether a result is real or a bug? Those skills transfer very directly, and you can build them at lots of places that do serious machine learning work.

If you're at a company training large models or running large-scale ML infrastructure, you'll pick up things that are hard to learn any other way: distributed training, working with big compute clusters, the practical intuitions about what breaks at scale. That's exactly the bottleneck we often hit. We have many more interesting research ideas than we have people who can execute on them quickly and well.

There are a couple of caveats. First, it matters what kind of engineering you're doing. If your job is mostly unrelated to machine learning, say front-end work or generic backend services, it's still useful but less directly so. You'd want to supplement it with ML projects on the side, like reimplementing papers, training small models yourself, or playing with fine-tuning and evaluation setups.

Second, I'd encourage people to keep engaging with the alignment side while they're doing that job. Read the papers, form your own opinions about which research directions seem promising, and maybe try small alignment-flavored projects. When you eventually apply, it's very helpful if you can show both that you're a strong engineer and that you've thought about the problem and actually care about it. That combination is what we're looking for.

So I'd say don't feel like you have to land on an alignment team on day one. A couple of years becoming a really excellent ML engineer somewhere else can make you a much stronger hire, as long as you keep your eye on where you ultimately want to go.

r001.rationale: The candidate says an outside research engineering job can be a good path and make someone a stronger hire, but does not state that candidates generally underestimate its value.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's actually a pretty good path, and I'd say it's probably one of the most common ways people end up on our team. The thing to understand is that research engineering is a really general skill set. If you've spent a couple of years at a strong ML lab, or honestly even a good tech company, building training pipelines, debugging distributed jobs, making experiments reproducible, getting good at reading other people's code and quickly figuring out why something isn't working, those skills transfer almost directly. The infrastructure and the day-to-day work on an alignment team isn't that different from the work on a capabilities team or an applied team. You're still running experiments on large models, you're still fighting with the same kinds of bugs.

What I'd push back on a little is the idea that you need to be at a specific company or doing a specific kind of research for it to count. The main thing I care about when I interview someone is: can they actually get things done? Can they take a somewhat vaguely specified research idea and turn it into a working experiment in a reasonable amount of time, and then notice when the results are telling them something unexpected? That's much more about having done a lot of real engineering under real constraints than about having worked on alignment per se.

The one caveat I'd add is that you should keep engaging with the alignment problem while you're there. Read the papers, think about what you'd want to work on, maybe do a small side project or a reproduction. Partly that's because it genuinely helps you figure out whether this is what you want to do, and partly because when you do apply, we want to see that you've thought about the problem and have your own views, not just that you're a strong engineer looking for a change. But if you have both, you're in a very good position. Honestly, I'd rather hire someone with two years of solid, battle-tested engineering experience who's been reading about alignment on the side than someone who jumped straight in without ever having shipped anything.

r001.rationale: The response calls another-company research engineering job a “pretty good path” and says it is one of the most common routes onto the team, but does not state that candidates generally underestimate its value.

astra-6.text:
I think that can be a really good way to prepare. A lot of what makes someone a strong research engineer is being able to implement ideas quickly, get experiments running reliably, and understand why they’re not working. You can develop those skills in a lot of places, and they transfer well to alignment research.

I would look at the specific role more than the company. Will you be working closely with good researchers? Will you get to run machine learning experiments and make decisions about what to try next? Will you get useful feedback on your work? Those are the things I’d want to optimize for.

But I also wouldn’t assume you need another job first. If you’re interested in working with us, apply. It’s hard to know from the outside whether you’re ready, and you don’t have to make that judgment entirely on your own.

r001.rationale: The response says another research engineering job can be a good way to prepare, but does not state that candidates generally underestimate its value.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that can be a really good way to prepare. A lot of the work on alignment requires strong engineering skills: being able to implement an experiment, debug it, and figure out why the results aren’t what you expected. You can develop those skills in a research engineering role elsewhere, especially if you’re working closely with researchers on machine learning.

The main thing I’d look for is whether you’ll actually be learning the skills you want to build. Will you get to run experiments? Will you have people around you who can give you good feedback? Taking a job like that can make sense, but I wouldn’t think of it as a prerequisite. If you’re interested in joining our team, you can also just apply, and we can figure out whether there’s a good fit.
